The implications of the above are as follows: Westmoreland's lower level of coal production (Scenario 1) will be able to absorb all available local labor (principally Crow) through 1980 while simultaneously providing a small but steady stimulus to the growth of Hardin. After 1980, however, the supply of local labor will once again begin to exceed the demand, and the Crow unemployment rate will begin to increase sharply. It appears that other development totalling about 20 million tons of coal per year, if begun around 1980, would be able to absorb local excess labor without generating large migration-related impacts on Hardin. Finally, another similar increase in coal production around 1985 would assure full utilization of local labor well into the 1990's.
The idea here is not to suggest a development strategy, but rather to make two points:
The level of labor demand associated with the Scenario 1 level of development by Westmoreland Resources and other substantial Crow coal development (AF-2) appears to be necessary if the projected rapid increases in the local labor supply are to be fully utilized;
This level of demand will not, however be necessary until the late 1980's; and if this level of demand materializes too soon (i. e., in the late 1970's), there will have to be substantial importation of labor, and Hardin will undergo the associated impacts.
